passage: When readers began, in large numbers, to write and circulate their own stories about the characters of popular novels and television series, the reaction from some authors was indignation. The characters were theirs, they said; to send them on adventures their creators had never imagined, to pair them with new lovers or to bring the dead back to life was a kind of trespass. Defenders of the practice replied with equal heat that a story, once released into the world, belongs to those who love it, and that the fans who keep a fictional world alive with their own inventions have a better claim to it than the person who merely began it. Both sides, I think, have misdescribed what is at stake.

Consider first how unusual the authors' position is, historically speaking. For most of the history of storytelling, retelling was the ordinary way in which stories lived. The same heroes passed from one teller to another, gaining episodes, companions and endings along the way; a poet who took up an old legend was expected to change it, and was admired for the changes. The idea that a fictional person belongs to a single creator, and that others may not set that person in new situations, took shape alongside printing, markets for books and laws that made authorship a form of property. It is not a natural fact about stories, though it now feels like one. Fan writers, from this angle, are less the vandals of a settled order than the late heirs of a much older one.

Yet the fans' champions claim too much when they turn this history into a counter-theory of ownership. To say that a story belongs to those who love it is still to speak of belonging, merely moving the title deeds from one party to another. What the older practice suggests is rather that stories are not the sort of thing that is owned in the first place, though particular tellings are. An author can reasonably object to having her text copied and sold under someone else's name, or to having her own work altered and passed off as hers. It is much harder to see what she loses when a reader imagines her characters on another afternoon, so long as no one mistakes that afternoon for one she wrote. The distinction between a text and a world is precisely the one that both sides have blurred.

There is an irony here that deserves notice. Fan communities, which began by contesting an author's exclusive authority, have often developed authorities of their own. Long debates arise over what counts as 'canon', over which inventions are faithful and which are betrayals, and newcomers who ignore the accumulated rules can be treated with a severity that few authors would dare to show their readers. In such moments the community reproduces, on a smaller scale, the very proprietary attitude it set out to resist, as though the impulse to fix a story and guard its boundaries were not peculiar to authors but a temptation that comes with loving any story at all.

None of this settles every case, and there are surely retellings that wound in ways the distinction does not capture, as when a living author's characters are put to uses she finds degrading. But it does suggest a more useful question than the one with which the quarrel began, which asked whose story it is. The better question is what each kind of claim protects: the integrity of a particular telling, which deserves defence, or the boundaries of an imagined world, which, on the evidence of the long history of storytelling, have never been defensible for long.

passage: The phrase most people use for the overland trade between China and the Mediterranean is a nineteenth-century coinage, and it carries a picture with it: a single road, and on it long caravans of camels carrying silk from one end of Asia to the other. The picture is attractive and largely misleading, for very few goods, and fewer merchants, made the whole journey. What existed instead was a chain of overlapping regional circuits, each worked by traders who knew their own stretch of desert, mountain and oasis intimately and knew little of what lay beyond it.

In such a system a bale of silk might change hands many times between the place where it was woven and the place where it was worn. Each exchange added a margin, which is one reason why goods from the far end of the chain were so costly, and each was made between people who had reason to trust one another because they met repeatedly. The merchant in an oasis town did not need to know the distant market where the silk would end up; he needed to know the caravan leader who would buy it from him and the one who had sold it to him. Long-distance trade, on this view, was an accumulation of short-distance relationships.

This has consequences that the romantic image hides. First, the system was more resilient than a single road would have been: when war or banditry closed one segment, goods could often find a way round it through neighbouring circuits, and trade slowed rather than stopped. Second, knowledge travelled poorly along the chain even when goods travelled well, and buyers at one end often held fanciful beliefs about where their luxuries came from, because no one they dealt with had seen the source. Third, those who profited most were frequently neither the producers nor the final buyers but the middlemen at the junctions where circuits met, whose cities grew rich on the margin.

It would be wrong to conclude that no one crossed the whole distance. Pilgrims, envoys and a few adventurous traders made extraordinary journeys, and some left accounts that are still read. But these travellers are remembered precisely because they were exceptional, and their fame has shaped our picture of the ordinary trade far more than the ordinary trade itself, which left few memoirs. A history built on the exceptional journey will see a road; a history built on the routine exchange will see a web, and it is the web that explains how the trade actually worked.

passage: It is often said that the phonograph and its successors simply made music available, carrying performances that had been confined to concert halls into the homes of people who would never have heard them. The claim is true as far as it goes, and the gain it describes is enormous: a listener in a small town can now hear more music in a month than a devoted concertgoer of earlier centuries could hope to hear in years. But the image of recording as a window, through which the listener observes a performance that would have happened in much the same way anyway, conceals the way recording altered both the performance and the act of listening.

Consider first what repetition does. A live performance is heard once; its slips pass and are forgotten, and its moments of risk are experienced as risk. A recording is heard again and again, and on the tenth hearing a wrong note or a wavering tone is no longer a passing accident but a permanent blemish. Performers who recorded learned that what was acceptable, even exciting, in a hall could become intolerable on disc. As editing techniques improved, it became possible to assemble a single flawless performance from many takes, and the flawless performance became the standard against which the live one was measured.

Listeners, in turn, came to the concert hall carrying recordings in their heads. Many now know a work first, and sometimes only, through one recorded interpretation, and they hear a live performance as a departure from it. This is a curious inversion. The recording was meant to be a copy of the performance; it has become, for many listeners, the original, and the performance its imperfect copy. Some performers have responded by playing more cautiously, aiming at the clean surface that audiences have learned to expect, at the cost of the spontaneity that once distinguished the live event.

It would be wrong to treat this as a simple story of decline. Recording has also allowed listeners to compare interpretations in a way no earlier audience could, and it has preserved musical traditions that might otherwise have vanished with their last practitioners. The point is rather that recording is not neutral. A technology that lets us hear the same performance indefinitely changes what we think a performance is for, and an account of modern musical life that leaves this out has mistaken a transformation for a mere extension.

passage: Collective security is one of those ideas that seem obviously right until one asks what they require. The principle is that an attack on any member of an international system is to be treated as an attack on all, so that every aggressor faces the combined strength of everyone else. Against this, the older practice of the balance of power looks cynical: states align against whichever power threatens to dominate, and they change sides as readily as the threat shifts, guided by interest rather than by any judgement about who is in the right.

The appeal of collective security lies in its impartiality, and so does its weakness. For the scheme to work, states must be willing to fight an aggressor regardless of who it is, which means fighting, if necessary, a friend, a major trading partner or a power whose goodwill they need elsewhere. They must also be willing to fight over places where they have no interest at all, because the principle admits no distinction between an attack that matters to them and one that does not. This is a great deal to ask of governments that answer to their own citizens, and the interwar experience suggests that, when the moment came, many would not pay the price. An organisation founded on the principle found its members ready to condemn aggression and reluctant to resist it.

The balance of power asks less and so delivers more reliably, at least within its narrower aims. It does not require states to care about aggression as such, only about the rise of a power that could threaten them, and so it draws on motives that governments actually have. But its reliability comes at a price. Because it attends only to the distribution of strength, it is indifferent to the fate of small states whose conquest does not upset the balance; it can tolerate, and has often arranged, the partition of a weak country as a way of keeping the strong ones satisfied. Stability is its aim, and justice enters only by accident.

The lesson is not that one principle should replace the other, but that each supplies what the other lacks. A norm against aggression, however imperfectly enforced, gives resistance to an expanding power a public justification and makes it easier to assemble allies who would hesitate to act on calculation alone. Balancing, in turn, supplies the motive that the norm cannot generate by itself. Orders that have lasted have usually combined the two, borrowing their legitimacy from the first and their enforcement from the second, and the mistake of the reformers who championed collective security was to imagine that legitimacy could do the work of both.

passage: When an automated system fails and a human operator fails to rescue it, the official account usually ends with the words 'human error'. The phrase is accurate in a narrow sense, since a person did do the wrong thing, but it hides the way the situation was produced. Automation is typically introduced to take over the parts of a task that are routine and well understood. What remains for the human is whatever the designers could not automate: the rare, ambiguous, fast-moving situations in which the machine gives up or behaves strangely. The person is thus left with the hardest part of the job, and is expected to perform it suddenly, after long periods of doing almost nothing.

Those long periods matter. Skill at controlling a process is kept alive by exercising it, and an operator who has spent months watching a screen rather than flying, steering or adjusting will have less of it than one who did the work by hand. Worse, the automation removes the everyday experience through which people build an intuitive model of how the system behaves, so that when something goes wrong they must reason about it from first principles, under pressure, with alarms sounding. Monitoring is also something human beings do badly. Attention drifts when nothing happens for hours, and the more reliable the machine, the longer the stretches in which nothing happens.

The result is a curious inversion. The better the automation works in ordinary conditions, the less prepared its human supervisors may be for the extraordinary ones, and the more surprising their failure will look when it comes. Calling that failure human error locates the fault in the individual at the very moment when the design of the whole arrangement deserves scrutiny.

None of this is a case against automation, which has removed a great deal of tedium and many kinds of mistake. It is a case for designing automated systems around the people who must step in when they fail. That might mean having operators run the process manually at regular intervals so that their skill does not decay, building displays that show what the machine is doing and why rather than only whether it is working, or deciding deliberately that some tasks should remain shared even when they could be fully automated. Such measures cost efficiency in the short run. Their justification is that the moments they prepare for, although rare, are the ones in which the most is at stake.

passage: The commonest objection to free verse is that it is merely prose with the margins moved. Take away the rhyme and the regular metre, the objection runs, and nothing distinguishes a poem from a paragraph except the typographer's decision to stop each line short of the edge of the page. If that decision is arbitrary, the poem is a pretence; if it is not, the objector would like to know what principle governs it, and a vague appeal to the poet's ear or instinct will not satisfy him.

The question deserves a better answer than poets usually give it, and the principle, where there is one, is that the line is a unit of attention. A reader pauses, however slightly, at the end of a line, and in that pause whatever the line has said is briefly complete. A sentence broken across two lines is therefore read twice: once as the line presents it and once as the sentence finally does. Consider a line that ends 'she said she would not leave', followed by one that begins 'the house until the rain had stopped'. For the length of the pause the woman refuses to leave at all; the next line shrinks the refusal to a matter of weather. Neither reading cancels the other; the poem holds the larger refusal and the smaller one together, and prose, which delivers its sentences whole, cannot easily do this.

Line breaks also govern pace, since a poem made of short lines slows the reader, weighting each word with a pause, while long lines carry her forward faster than the sense alone would. Where metre once supplied a regular beat against which a poet could set the natural stresses of speech, the free verse poet works with the silence at the ends of lines, which is a cruder instrument than metre but not a negligible one, and which has the compensating advantage that it can be varied from line to line without breaking any rule.

None of this shows that the objection is always wrong. A good deal of what is published as free verse is broken into lines for no reason a reader could recover, and in such cases the objection is simply correct: the lines could be run together without loss. A fair test is exactly that: set the poem out as prose, read it again, and ask what has gone. If nothing is lost, if no meaning that the breaks created has vanished and no pace has been flattened, then the breaks were decoration. What the test cannot do is condemn the form as such, since in the poems that pass it the breaks turn out to have been doing work that the prose version cannot preserve.

passage: The most familiar objection to industrial policy is that governments cannot pick winners. Officials, the objection runs, have neither the information nor the incentives to know which industries will flourish; investors risking their own money are better placed to judge, and when the state substitutes its judgement for theirs it will usually back the wrong horses and keep feeding them long after the race is lost. The objection has history on its side, in the sense that the record of state-backed ventures includes many expensive failures. But it rests on a picture of the problem that deserves closer inspection.

The picture is one in which the menu of possible industries is known and the only question is which item to choose. Investors, in this picture, already know what a country could produce profitably, and the government's error is to overrule them. Yet for an economy trying to move into activities it has never undertaken, no one possesses this knowledge. Whether a particular region can grow cut flowers for export, assemble electronic components or write software for foreign clients depends on a mass of local particulars, from the reliability of the roads to the habits of the workforce, that can be learned only by trying. An investor asked in advance would have no better basis for a forecast than an official; both would be guessing. The relevant knowledge is not hidden in investors' heads waiting to be consulted; it does not yet exist.

Producing it is costly, and here the market's usual advantages turn against it. The first entrepreneur to discover that a product can be made profitably in a given place bears the full cost of the experiment if it fails, but if it succeeds, others can copy the discovery cheaply, entering the industry once its viability has been shown. The pioneer thus bears the losses of failure while sharing the rewards of success, and rational investors will undertake fewer such experiments than the economy as a whole would want. The case for public involvement follows not from officials knowing more than investors, but from no one knowing enough and the cost of finding out being borne unevenly.

If this is right, the objection about picking winners is aimed at the wrong target. A policy of supporting discovery will back many ventures that fail; that is what experiment means, and a programme that never failed would be one that was taking no risks. Measured by the share of its bets that pay off, a sound programme of discovery may look worse than a timid one. The genuine danger lies elsewhere: support, once given, may become impossible to withdraw, so that the losers are kept alive at public expense. What matters is less the ability to pick winners than the ability to let losers go, and the second ability, though rarely discussed, is at least as hard to acquire as the first.

The approach has a cost of its own, and it would be dishonest to minimise it. Discovering what local firms could do requires officials to work closely with them, to learn what obstacles they face and what help would remove them. The same closeness that yields information also invites capture, in which those meant to be overseen come to set the terms. Officials who meet the same managers every month will find it hard to tell them, when a review date arrives, that support is ending. There is no formula that separates collaboration from collusion, only practices, such as public criteria and fixed review dates, that make the difference easier to see. That is a weaker guarantee than the advocates of industrial policy would like, but it is a stronger one than its critics usually assume.

passage: When a news organisation discovers that it has published something false, the conventional remedy is a correction: a short notice, often printed some days later and some pages away from the original, stating that the earlier report was wrong. Few people defend the correction as adequate, but the usual complaint, that corrections are too small and too late, misses the more interesting difficulty. Even a correction that is prominent and prompt may fail, and it may fail because of what a retraction asks the mind to do. The problem, in other words, is psychological before it is editorial, and editorial remedies that ignore this are likely to disappoint.

Consider a report that a fire in a warehouse was caused by paint and chemicals stored carelessly in a back room. A day later the paper announces that no such materials were present. The reader is now asked to give up the only explanation offered for the fire and to put nothing in its place. Minds do not handle this well. People tend to understand events as chains of cause and effect, and a chain with a link removed does not simply grow shorter; it breaks. An account with a missing link is uncomfortable, and when asked later why the warehouse burned, many readers reach for the explanation they were told to discard, not because they disbelieve the correction but because the correction left them with no story at all. The false claim survives because it was doing work that the retraction did not take over.

If this is right, the remedy lies less in the size of the correction than in its content. A retraction that supplies an alternative account, stating what did cause the fire, or at least what the investigators now think likely, gives the reader somewhere to go. Where no alternative is yet known, the correction can at least explain why the original claim was made and why it seemed plausible, so that the discarded belief is accounted for rather than merely forbidden. There is a familiar worry that repeating a false claim, even in order to deny it, will make it more familiar and so more believable. The worry is reasonable, but it should not lead editors to issue vague notices that never say what was wrong; a denial that does not name its target cannot replace anything.

None of this makes corrections easy, and it does not excuse the haste that produces most errors in the first place. A newsroom that publishes a confident causal story before the facts are in has created a problem that no notice can fully undo, since the first explanation a reader meets enjoys an advantage that later ones must work to overcome. Readers who met the false cause first will often have repeated it to others, built further conclusions upon it, and forgotten where they heard it. The lesson for reporters is therefore double: be slower to supply a cause, and, when one has been supplied wrongly, be quicker to supply a better one.

passage: For most of the twentieth century, medicine described its relationship with microbes in the language of war. Bacteria invaded, the immune system defended, and antibiotics were weapons that wiped out the enemy. The metaphor was not idle decoration. It organised research around identifying a single culprit for each disease and finding a means of killing it, and that programme saved an enormous number of lives.

The study of the microbes that live in and on healthy bodies has made the war metaphor look crude. Most of these organisms are not enemies; many are useful, helping to digest food, train the immune system and occupy space that harmful species would otherwise take. An ecological vocabulary has therefore become popular: the body is a habitat, the gut is a crowded ecosystem, and health is a matter of the right community rather than the absence of germs. This vocabulary explains things the older one could not. It makes sense of why a broad course of antibiotics can be followed by a stubborn intestinal infection: by clearing out the resident species, the drug removes the competitors that had kept a harmful one in check. It also makes sense of why transferring gut bacteria from a healthy donor has proved effective against that very infection.

Yet the new metaphor carries risks of its own, and they are less often noticed because it sounds so benign. Ecology, popularly understood, suggests balance and harmony, as though every body had a single proper community to which it should be restored. Ecologists themselves are more cautious; real ecosystems have many stable states, change with season and disturbance, and do not come with a correct composition. The popular version has proved ideal for marketing. Products that promise to 'rebalance' the gut can borrow the authority of a serious science while specifying nothing that could be measured, and the vagueness of the promise protects it from ever being shown false.

The lesson is not that medicine should return to the language of war, nor that metaphors can be avoided. Every science thinks partly through images, and the choice is between images that sharpen questions and images that blur them. The ecological picture is valuable when it brings with it the working concepts of ecology, such as competition, succession and the effects of disturbance, which generate predictions that can be tested. It becomes a liability when it brings only the mood of ecology, a feeling of harmony that no experiment could ever contradict.

passage: Discussions of the unreliable narrator tend to treat it as a game of detection. A narrator tells us one thing, the novel quietly lets us see another, and the pleasure lies in catching the gap: the jealous husband who insists he is perfectly calm, the child who reports adult quarrels without understanding them. Critics have catalogued the signals by which such narrators give themselves away, the protest that is too insistent, the detail that contradicts a claim made a page earlier, and readers have learned to watch for them. On this account the device is a kind of puzzle, and a reader who has spotted the discrepancy has finished the work the book asked of her. The narrator was wrong; the reader, standing above him, is right.

This picture is not false, but it is thin. It assumes that behind every unreliable account there stands a reliable one, which the attentive reader reconstructs and then keeps. Yet the clues by which we detect a narrator's distortions are supplied by the same narrator. We infer that the husband is jealous from what he notices, what he repeats, what he cannot stop describing; we have no other witness. The true story we assemble is therefore itself an interpretation, built from the materials of the account we have decided to distrust, and we hold it with a confidence that the novel has done nothing to guarantee.

What the best uses of the device achieve, then, is not the replacement of a bad narrator by a good reader but a change in how the reader regards narration as such. Having learned to read one voice against itself, we begin to notice how much we ordinarily grant to voices that give no sign of strain: the calm third-person narrator of a realist novel, the memoirist, the friend recounting a quarrel. None of them is lying, perhaps, but all of them select, arrange and omit. The difference is one of degree rather than kind; the narrator we call reliable is simply one whose selections we have not thought to question. The unreliable narrator makes visible a condition that reliable narration merely conceals.

It must be admitted that not every novel built on an untrustworthy teller rises to this. Some use the device as a trapdoor, a revelation held back for the final chapters that turns everything before it into misdirection. Such books can be thrilling once. On a second reading, however, they tend to go flat, because the only question they posed has been answered. The novels that survive rereading are those in which the distrust never quite settles, in which the reader, having caught the narrator out, is left wondering what she herself has failed to see.

passage: Among the habits that journalists learn early is the instinct to give both sides. When a council proposes a new road, the reporter calls the residents who want it and the residents who do not; when a minister defends a policy, the opposition is asked to respond. The habit is a good one wherever the disagreement is about values or interests, because there the reporter has no standing to declare a winner, and readers are entitled to hear the competing cases at comparable length. To do otherwise would be to editorialise under the cover of reporting, settling a political question by the simple device of quoting only one side.

Difficulties arise when the same habit is carried over to questions of fact on which the evidence is heavily one-sided. Suppose that nearly all the researchers who study a question have reached one conclusion, and a handful dissent. A report that sets one scientist from each camp side by side, allotting them equal time, is scrupulously fair to the two individuals and seriously misleading about the state of knowledge. The reader, reasonably assuming that a newspaper does not stage contests between unequal parties, infers that the field is evenly split. Repeated over many reports, the impression hardens into a belief that the experts are hopelessly divided, and a reader may then feel free to choose whichever answer is more congenial. The format has communicated a falsehood that neither speaker uttered.

The obvious objection is that journalists are poorly placed to judge which scientific views are sound, and that the history of science contains majorities that turned out to be wrong. Both points are true, and neither rescues the practice. The reporter is not being asked to decide who is right, only to describe accurately how opinion within a field is distributed, which is itself a matter of fact that can be checked. And the occasional vindication of a lone dissenter is not a reason to present every dissenter as half the story; most minority positions in science are minority positions because the evidence has gone against them. If a dissent later prevails, it will be because the evidence changed, and the reporting can change with it.

What the critique of false balance requires, then, is not the exclusion of minority views but their placement. A dissenting researcher can be quoted, and quoted fairly, as a dissenter, with the reader told plainly how far that view departs from the field. What the reader should not be given is the impression, created by symmetry alone, that the dissenter speaks for half of those who know the subject. Nor does the critique apply where science is genuinely unsettled; there, presenting rival hypotheses side by side is exactly right. The skill it demands is harder than either reflexive balance or reflexive deference: it is the skill of knowing which kind of question one is reporting on.

passage: One of the first lessons of economics is that money is fungible. A rupee earned is the same as a rupee found, a rupee received as a gift or a rupee won at cards; since each can buy exactly what the others can, a rational person should be indifferent to where a sum came from and should spend it according to a single ranking of needs. This is what makes money so useful. It strips goods of their particular histories and renders them comparable, and it lets a stranger in one town trade with a stranger in another without either needing to know anything about the other's life.

Ordinary households, however, behave as though they had never heard the lesson. Coins for the temple are kept in a separate tin; a grandmother's gift to a newborn goes into a savings account that no one will touch for rent even in a hard month; the money a woman earns from tailoring is spent on her children's schooling, while her husband's wages go to food and the loan; a windfall is spent on a celebration that the same sum, arriving as salary, would never have funded. Money that arrives in one way is marked, set aside and spent in another, as though each sum carried a label that its owners were bound to respect. Nor are such habits confined to poor households; in one form or another they appear in families at every level of income.

The standard response is to call this mental accounting and to treat it as a lapse, a cognitive shortcut that serves people tolerably on the whole but leads them into avoidable errors. The errors are real. A family that keeps savings in a low-interest account reserved for a daughter's wedding while borrowing at a ruinous rate to repair the roof is paying heavily for a distinction that, in purely financial terms, does not exist. Yet to describe earmarking only as a mistake is to miss what it accomplishes. The grandmother's gift is set apart because it is a relationship as much as a sum: spending it on rent would feel like dissolving the bond it expressed. The tailor's earnings are spent on schooling because keeping them distinct allows her to claim, within the household, a sphere of decision that pooled money would not give her. Labels on money are the means by which people make it say something about who they are to one another.

It may be objected that this shows only that people attach feelings to money, not that money itself ceases to be fungible. In the market, after all, the tailor's rupee buys exactly what her husband's does, and no shopkeeper asks about its origin. The objection is correct about the shopkeeper. But it concedes the point that matters. Fungibility holds where people have agreed to ignore the histories of sums, as in impersonal trade, and fails where they have not, as in the household, the family ceremony and the circle of friends who lend to one another.

The single, featureless money of the textbook, then, is not a natural property of currency that social life afterwards distorts. It is an arrangement that holds in certain settings and that people are constantly unmaking elsewhere. To see this is not to deny that the arrangement is valuable, or that families sometimes pay dearly for their labels; it is to recognise that the indifference to origins which economics takes as its starting point is itself a social achievement, and a local one.

passage: For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, scholars who wrote about the history of writing liked to arrange the world's scripts on a ladder. At the bottom stood picture-writing, in which signs resembled the things they named; above it came scripts in which signs stood for whole words; above those, scripts whose signs stood for syllables; and at the summit, the alphabet, in which a few dozen letters represented the individual sounds of speech. The ladder told a story of progress toward economy and abstraction, and it rarely escaped notice that the peoples occupying the topmost rung were, in most such accounts, the authors' own.

The ladder has not survived scrutiny well. Its first difficulty is descriptive. The scripts it consigned to the lower rungs were seldom what it said they were: the characters of Chinese, often presented as pictures of things, are in large part compounds in which one component indicates meaning and another indicates, however loosely, sound. Such a script is not a halting step toward phonetic writing but a different and highly developed answer to the problem of recording a language. Its second difficulty is historical. The sequence it describes is, at best, the history of one lineage of scripts in one region, and to present it as the path that all writing must follow is to mistake a family tree for a law of nature.

The deeper difficulty concerns the standard of judgment. The ladder assumed that a script should be ranked by how few signs it needs, so that fewer signs meant a better system. Economy of inventory is a real virtue; a child learning an alphabet with regular spelling can sound out unfamiliar words within a few years, and few would deny that this is an advantage. But it is one criterion among several. A script that represents meaning directly can be read across spoken varieties that differ so much in pronunciation that their speakers cannot follow one another in conversation. A mixed system, such as the one used for Japanese, can show at a glance which parts of a sentence carry lexical content and which carry grammar, an aid to rapid reading once the system is mastered. And an alphabet is only as economical as its spelling permits; a language whose spelling has drifted far from its pronunciation, as English has, can oblige its learners to memorise many words almost as wholes.

None of this implies that scripts are equal in every respect or that the choice of script is unimportant. The costs of learning differ, and some of them fall heavily on those with the least schooling. A script deliberately devised in fifteenth-century Korea, whose letter shapes reflect how the sounds they represent are produced, was designed with exactly such learners in mind, and its designers evidently believed that some ways of writing were better than others for certain ends. That belief is a ranking of a kind, but it is a ranking relative to a purpose, which is precisely what the ladder lacked.

It is also worth noticing what the ladder's critics should not claim. To deny that the alphabet is the summit of writing is not to say that literacy rates owe nothing to scripts; they plainly owe something. It is to say that they owe much more to schools, to the availability of reading matter and to whether reading pays, and that societies with very different scripts have reached near-universal literacy once those conditions were in place. The ladder told us that the script was destiny. The record suggests it is closer to terrain: it shapes the route, but it does not decide who arrives.

passage: A long tradition in the philosophy of science treats explanation and prediction as two faces of one achievement. To explain why an event happened, on this view, is to show that it could have been expected, given the relevant laws and the conditions that held beforehand; to predict an event is to perform the same derivation before the event rather than after it. The symmetry is attractive because it makes explanation answerable to something. An explanation that could not, even in principle, have served as a prediction would seem to be no more than a story told after the fact. The view also promised a single standard for the whole of science, from astronomy, where eclipses are calculated centuries ahead, to clinical medicine, where a diagnosis is expected both to account for a patient's symptoms and to anticipate their course.

Yet the symmetry fails in both directions. A falling barometer reading is an excellent predictor of a coming storm, and anyone who knows the correlation can forecast the weather with it; but no one supposes that the barometer explains the storm. Both are effects of a drop in atmospheric pressure, and the reading earns its predictive power by riding on that common cause. Conversely, we can often explain what we could never have predicted. A geologist can say why a particular hillside gave way, pointing to saturated soil and a weakened layer of clay, without having been able to say beforehand that it would fail that week rather than in some other year. The explanation is sound even though the forecast was out of reach.

What these cases suggest is that explanation and prediction answer to different demands. A predictor need only be reliably connected with what it predicts; it does not matter how the connection arises. An explanation must identify what the outcome depends on: the factors such that, had they been different, the outcome would have been different too. The barometer fails that test, since a broken barometer would not have prevented the storm; the clay passes it, since firmer clay would have held the slope.

None of this makes prediction irrelevant to explanation. A claim about what an outcome depends on usually implies something about what would happen under other conditions, and checking those implications is how such claims are tested. A theory that explains everything and forbids nothing should make us suspicious. But the test is a check on an explanation, not its substance. To confuse the two is to mistake the evidence that an account is right for the thing that makes it an account at all.

passage: When collectors began, in the nineteenth century, to travel through the countryside writing down the songs of rural singers, they often approached their task as an act of rescue. The songs, they believed, were ancient and dying, and each singer they encountered was a damaged witness to an original that had once existed in a purer and more complete form. Variation between versions was evidence of decay: a verse forgotten here, a line garbled there, a tune that had wandered from its proper shape. The collector's responsibility, accordingly, was to compare the surviving fragments and reconstruct, as far as the evidence permitted, the song as it had existed before the damage began.

This picture borrowed its method from the editing of ancient manuscripts, where it makes good sense. A classical text was written once by a particular author, and later copies really are more or less faithful to it. A folk song is a fundamentally different kind of object. It was never fixed in a single authoritative form; it existed only in individual performances, each of which was shaped by the singer's memory, temperament and taste, and by the particular audience and occasion. A singer who shortened a ballad for a restless crowd, or changed the name of a town to one her listeners knew, was not corrupting a text. She was doing what singers of such songs had always done, and what had made the songs worth keeping.

Seen this way, variation is not the symptom of a song's decline but the very mechanism of its survival. Songs that could be adapted to unfamiliar places and new purposes travelled widely; songs that resisted such adaptation were gradually forgotten. The very versions the collectors regarded as degraded were often the ones in which a song was most alive, because they showed it being fitted to the people who still sang it. There is an irony here. By printing a single standard text, often assembled from several singers, the collectors gave the songs the fixed form they had never had, and later performers sometimes learned from the printed page instead of from other singers.

It would nevertheless be unfair to dismiss the collectors' work on this account. Without their notebooks a great many songs would be irrecoverably lost, and some of them took care to record variants and the names of the singers they heard. The lesson is narrower. A record of oral music is valuable precisely to the extent that it preserves the variety which the collectors' theory taught them to regard as noise.

passage: We tend to think of the passport as a document that lets people travel. It is the thing we pack and check twice before leaving for the airport, and losing it abroad feels like being stranded. Yet the history of the passport suggests that its first purpose was not to open borders but to give states a means of closing them selectively. A document that certifies who you are, and which state answers for you, is above all a tool for deciding who may enter, who may leave, and who may be turned back.

For much of the nineteenth century, a traveller could cross many European frontiers without being asked for papers at all. Controls existed, but they were patchy, and in several countries they were relaxed as railways made movement faster and cheaper. The First World War changed this. Governments anxious about spies, deserters and the flight of men of fighting age began demanding documents at every crossing, and when the war ended the requirement was not withdrawn. What had been introduced as an emergency measure became the ordinary condition of international travel, and the expectation that every person should belong to exactly one state, and carry proof of it, hardened into common sense. Few people now remember that it was ever otherwise.

None of this makes the passport simply an instrument of control. For the person who holds it, it is also a claim on protection: it entitles the bearer to return home and to seek help from the officials of the issuing state when abroad. The predicament of stateless people, who have no government willing to vouch for them, shows how much that claim is worth. Without it, a person can be refused entry everywhere and expelled from wherever he happens to be.

The more uncomfortable point is that the protection is unevenly distributed. Two travellers standing in the same queue may carry documents of identical design and very different power, one admitting its holder to most of the world without a visa, the other inviting suspicion at every desk. What the passport records, then, is not only identity but rank in an order of states, an accident of birth that the individual did little to earn and can rarely change. Nor is that rank settled by anything the traveller does at the desk; it is negotiated between governments, through visa agreements and reciprocal arrangements, long before any individual reaches the frontier. To call the document a passport to freedom is to describe the experience of those whose papers happen to work.

passage: For most of its history the word 'computer' named an occupation rather than a machine. Observatories, survey offices and, later, engineering firms employed rooms of people whose work consisted of carrying out long calculations, often for tables of positions, tides or trajectories that others would use. It is tempting to treat these workers as a quaint prelude to the real story, a stopgap that lasted only until electronics arrived. That reading gets the relation backwards. The electronic computer did not introduce the idea of mechanical calculation into a world that lacked it; it inherited an idea that human computing offices had already worked out in detail.

The key feature of such offices was not the arithmetic skill of any individual but the way the work was organised. A planner with mathematical training would break a difficult problem into a sequence of simple steps, write those steps on printed sheets, and hand the sheets to workers who needed to know only how to add, subtract and look up values in a table. The workers did not have to understand why a step was there, and the scheme was in fact designed so that they would not need to. Errors were caught not by insight but by procedure: two people would compute the same column independently, and any disagreement sent the column back. What was being built, in effect, was a method in which correctness no longer depended on anyone grasping the whole.

Seen this way, much of what we think of as distinctive about programming was already present. The separation between the person who designs a procedure and the agent who executes it, the reduction of judgement to rules, the checking of results by redundancy rather than by understanding: all of these were practices before they were properties of machines. When the first electronic machines were built, their designers could borrow not only mathematical techniques from the computing offices but also a whole conception of what it meant to make a calculation reliable.

None of this is to say that the machines merely did faster what people had done slowly. Speed of the magnitude electronics provided changed which problems were worth posing at all; calculations that would have occupied a room of workers for years became routine, and whole fields grew up around them. But the continuity matters, because it reminds us that the habit of treating thought as something that can be divided, written down and handed to an executor who need not understand it is a social invention before it is a technical one. Its consequences, good and bad, were visible in offices long before they were visible on screens.

passage: The idea that some jobs require workers to manage their own feelings, and not merely their hands or their minds, has travelled a long way from its origins in the study of flight attendants and debt collectors. It now turns up in discussions of nursing, teaching, retail and call centres, and even of the unpaid work of keeping a family cheerful. This expansion has drawn a predictable objection: if every job involves some management of emotion, the critics say, then the concept marks out nothing in particular. A surgeon must stay calm, a lawyer must appear confident, and a builder who loses his temper with clients will not keep them; are these, too, emotional labourers?

The objection is fair against the loose use of the term, but it misses what the original idea was pointing at. The distinction was never between jobs that involve feeling and jobs that do not. It was between feeling that a worker manages according to her own judgement and feeling whose display is specified, monitored and sold by someone else. The surgeon's calm serves the operation and is left to her; nobody scripts it. The call-centre agent, by contrast, may be told how often to use the customer's name, scored on the warmth of her voice, and disciplined for a sigh. The emotion is part of the product, and the employer, not the worker, sets its terms.

Seen this way, the concept is narrower than its popular use suggests, but also sharper. It directs attention not to the presence of emotion at work but to its ownership, and it suggests where the cost of such work lies. Most people can smile at a stranger without harm; the difficulty arises when the smile must be produced on demand, for hours, regardless of how the worker is treated, and when failing to produce it is a disciplinary matter. One would expect work of this kind to produce a fatigue unlike ordinary tiredness, and perhaps an uncertainty about which friendly feelings are one's own.

None of this implies that friendliness in service is a sham, or that customers who enjoy it are dupes. Many workers take pride in easing a stranger's day, and a scripted greeting can be delivered with real goodwill. The point is that goodwill freely given and goodwill required by contract are different things, even when they look identical from the other side of the counter, and a concept that cannot tell them apart has lost the very thing that made it worth having.

passage: When a job that was once filled by school leavers begins to advertise for graduates, the usual explanation is that the work has become more demanding. Machines have taken over the routine tasks, the story goes, and what remains calls for the analytical habits that only a university can supply. There is something to this. Some occupations really have changed beyond recognition, and an office clerk today handles systems that would have baffled a clerk of fifty years ago. But the explanation is offered far more often than it is checked, and when one looks at what people in many of these jobs actually do, the change in the work is often modest beside the change in the paperwork required to get it.

A more economical account treats the degree less as a certificate of skill than as a ticket in a queue. When few people held degrees, an employer who asked for one was selecting a small group who were, on average, more persistent and better connected than the rest. As degrees became common, the same requirement no longer separated anyone, and employers who wanted to keep selecting raised the bar again, asking for a master's where a bachelor's had once sufficed. Each employer is behaving sensibly; it is merely using the cheapest filter available. Yet the sum of these sensible choices resembles a crowd at a parade in which everyone stands on tiptoe: no one sees better than before, and everyone is more tired.

The costs of this arrangement are not evenly spread. Students from families that can afford several years of fees and forgone earnings keep pace with the rising bar; those who cannot are shut out of work they could perfectly well perform. A requirement introduced in the name of competence thus ends up rewarding the capacity to pay for time. Meanwhile the graduates themselves often discover that much of what they studied is barely used in the job, and that what the employer valued was the signal rather than the substance.

None of this is an argument against education, which has goods that no labour market can measure. It is an argument against confusing two things that the word 'qualification' runs together: what a person can do, and how long a person has been able to stay in school. Some employers have begun to test applicants directly on the tasks the job involves. Where this is done, an awkward question comes into view, namely whether the degree requirement it replaces was ever a guarantee of quality or merely a habit that nobody had thought to examine.

passage: Few historical lessons are repeated as confidently as the one drawn from the settlement that followed the First World War. A harsh peace, the lesson runs, breeds resentment, and resentment breeds the next war; a generous peace, by contrast, turns yesterday's enemy into tomorrow's partner. The lesson is attractive because it joins morality to prudence. It tells victors that magnanimity is not only noble but wise, and that they can secure the future simply by being kind. It also offers a single, memorable explanation for one of the great catastrophes of the last century, and explanations of that kind are hard to dislodge once they have settled into textbooks and speeches.

The trouble is that the record does not sort so neatly. Some severe settlements have held for generations, because the defeated party was too weak to overturn them and the victors remained willing to enforce their terms. Some lenient ones have failed, because the loser read leniency as a sign that it had not really been beaten and that a second attempt might succeed. What such cases suggest is that severity and generosity are the wrong variables to watch. A settlement lasts when its terms match the actual balance of strength, and when the powers that wrote it remain prepared to uphold it.

By this measure, the worst settlement is not the harshest but the one that combines harsh terms with a weak will to enforce them. Such a peace gives the defeated every reason to resent the order and no reason to fear challenging it. Its demands are heavy enough to humiliate, yet the victors, tired of war and divided among themselves, let them be evaded piece by piece, until the settlement has lost both its authority and its power to deter. Much of the interwar story can be told in this way, as a failure less of severity than of follow-through.

This is not an argument for cruelty dressed up as realism. Generosity has a real role, but it works best after the defeat has been made unmistakable, when it can be read as the confidence of a winner rather than the hesitation of a power unsure of its victory. Offering a defeated state a path back into the community of nations, through trade, membership of institutions and the eventual lifting of restrictions, gives it a stake in the order that no amount of punishment can create. The point is only that kindness must rest on a settlement that is clear about who won and is backed by someone willing to say so.
